129	### Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object
130	
131	This is the library's own way for `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char`, applied to the five number traits. It is way C plus one change of the library's text.
132	
133	**On `ZZ32`.**
134	
135	    value object ZZ32 extends { AnyIntegral, Integral[\ZZ32\], Index }
136	        coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = v.asZZ32
137	        asFloat(self): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToDouble")
138	        opr =(self, b:ZZ32):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intEQ")
139	        ...
140	    end
141	
142	`Int` is gone. The `excludes` and `comprises` clauses go too: an object excludes every type that it does not extend. The class:
143	
144	    final class ZZ32 { final int val; ... }     (one declaration, one class, one name)
145	
146	**On `Boolean`.** Nothing changes: it is already this shape. The same for `Char`, `NN32`, `RR32`.
147	
148	**On `String`.** Nothing changes: `String` has four objects, so it stays a trait, as in way C.
149	
150	**On `Float`.** `value object RR64` takes `Float`'s 146 lines. About 50 bodies of `trait RR64` go: `opr +(self,b:RR64):RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` and its like (`FortressLibrary.fss:408-504`; 57 lines of the trait hold `asFloat(self)`). They served when `RR64` had four subtypes. Today every `RR64` is a `Float`, so `Float`'s own `+` is always the more specific one, and by the dispatch rule these bodies never run. By reading; no test shows it.
151	
152	**Why the split is there.** It was made for two reasons, and both are gone.
153	
154	- Maessen split `ZZ32` on 2008-07-15 so that `IntLiteral` could be a subtype of `ZZ32` (`fca589bbb0`: "ZZ32 is now a trait, with subtypes Int and IntLiteral"). The numerals have their own types now (P-173, P-174), and `IntLiteral` left the library.
155	- The other traits had subtypes by nesting: `trait ZZ64 ... comprises { Long, ZZ32 }` at the team's last commit. The tower is flat now (P-43).
156	
157	So each of the five traits has exactly one object, and the split serves nothing that the record names.
158	
159	**What blocks it.** Under walk, an object with native values must be in a native component. `FortressLibrary` is not one. So the five move into `FortressBuiltin`, beside `NN32` and `RR32`, or walk learns one more place. The names `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go: by a grep of whole words, the library names them on 4, 4, 41, 4 and 4 lines, almost all in their own declarations. A few tests name one as a type, among them `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:31-35`, `tests/NativeHelperFloatCarriedWalk.fss:5-6` and `compiler_tests/XXXNativeHelperOwnUnsignedLongCompiled.fss:8`. No model line does.
160	
161	**What it changes.**
162	
163	- The library's text: five objects deleted, five traits made objects and moved, about 600 lines moved, about 50 dead bodies deleted.
164	- Walk: five constructor classes renamed; the reading of F-344 and the ilk names of F-328 become needless for the numbers and stay for the strings.
165	- The code generator: as way C, without the rule for a trait with one comprised object, and without W12's rule for the numbers.
166	- The run-time classes and the loader: as way C.
167	- The tests: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk` and `tests/FlatTowerRungF` change where they name the objects. The checker's count and the distance are run again. I did not run them: this is the first probe to make before the way is chosen.
168	
169	**Speed later.** As way C, and a little more: one declaration per operator instead of two, so the dispatch method of `+` has one arm less for each number type, and the static type is the class with no rule in between.
170	
171	**Undo.** The merge is mechanical each way, but it changes text that the team wrote. From C, it can be taken at any time. From D back to C, the objects are written again.
172	
173	**The team's texts.** For: `NN32` (Steele, 2008), `RR32` (Ryu, 2008), `Boolean` and `Char` are this shape in the library; the prelude's first number types were objects (Flood, 2009-03-03); the library's own complaint about `Float` against `RR64` (below); every peer. Against: the specification's api style shows a built-in type as a trait with hidden comprised types; the split is the team's text, though its reasons are gone.

111	
112	## 6. The run: the second JVM and the class loader
113	
114	**The second JVM.** `bin/fortress run` hands off to `bin/run`, which launches
115	`com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper` (`bin/fortress:16-18`,
116	`bin/run:41`). The class path puts `bytecode_cache`, `bytecode_cache/*` and
117	`nativewrapper_cache` **ahead** of the tool class path
118	(`bin/run_classpath:26`).
119	
120	**The trap in that ordering.** If the library jars are not in
121	`bytecode_cache`, the loader silently falls back to frozen stubs compiled from
122	checked-in Java sources into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/` — an older
123	snapshot of `CompilerBuiltin` — and the program dies with a
124	`NoSuchMethodError` on a method that plainly exists in the `.fss`
125	(`repo-internals.md:162-182`; `modules-and-phases.md` B.13). The cure is to
126	compile the five library components in order first; the recipe is in
127	`repo-internals.md:170-180`. This is a cache problem misread as a compiler bug
128	for years (`repo-internals.md:152-160`).
129	
130	**What `MainWrapper` does.** It first stashes the program's arguments in a
131	static field rather than passing them. It then initializes the named component's
132	class, and the class of each component that it uses, through
133	`InstantiatingClassloader.ONLY`, in a root task (F-348). Then it invokes the
134	named class's no-argument `main` (`runtimeSystem/MainWrapper.java:19, 30-46,
135	94-98`, at climb batch 30's landing, `d89fc0fda4`).
136	
137	**The class loader is where compiled Fortress stops being ordinary bytecode.**
138	`InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` (2,946 lines in the file; the method at
139	`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178`) examines the class *name*
140	for markers and, for most of them, **generates** the class instead of reading
141	it (`:227-296`):
142	
143	- a tuple RTTI class, an arrow RTTI class (`:227-232`);
144	- a generic function instance, by reading the template and rewriting it
145	  (`:233-242`);
146	- a closure (`:243-244`);
147	- for a name in oxford or angle brackets: arrow interfaces and their abstract
148	  and wrapped forms, tuple types, concrete and "any" tuples, union types, and —
149	  the general case — an instantiation of a generic template
150	  (`:245-280`);
151	- an RTTI class, translated to flush out symbolic references (`:281-290`);
152	- otherwise, the bytes as they are (`:292-294`).
153	
154	**What the rewriting is.** `Instantiater` is an ASM `ClassVisitor` holding two
155	substitution maps, one for types and one for operators; `visit` replaces the
156	class's own name, its superclass and each interface with the substituted name
157	(`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:26-38, 47-58`). The bracket and mangling
158	conventions are `runtimeSystem/Naming.java` (1,203 lines).
159	
160	**What it does not do.** *Instantiation renames; it does not change
161	representation* (`modules-and-phases.md` B.11, and the same conclusion in the
162	map's summary, `map/README.md` §2). There is no mechanism for giving one
163	instantiation a different field shape from another: the expando hook that would
164	do it is a stub, `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }`
165	(`InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-171`). A probe in the array review confirms
166	that stamping cannot produce a `double[]` field
167	(`array-design-review.md` Q4).
168	
169	**What it does with a size in a type, today.** The compiler mangles a size into
170	the instantiation name: `NamingCzar` maps `KindNat` and each `IntArg` to the
171	tag `Naming.XL_INTNAT` (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:1826-1832`, `:1888-1910`).
172	Nothing reads it back. The runtime's generic RTTI class holds one field per
173	static parameter, all typed as type RTTI, and the only kind the runtime
174	consults is `opr` (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1600-1622`;
175	`Naming.java:95-108`); `XL_INTNAT` is declared at `Naming.java:213` and that is
176	its only runtime mention. Measured consequence: a `nat` used in *value*
177	position compiles to a `getstatic` of a class the loader cannot produce and
178	dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError`
179	(`array-design-review.md` §1b, probe 6). And the code generator refuses a size
180	in an `extends` clause before that, with
181	`CompilerError("Only emitting RTTI for types right now")`
182	(`CodeGen.java:5793`).
183	
184	**The rest of the runtime.** A compiled program's entry class extends
185	`FortressExecutable`, whose static initializer creates one work-stealing pool
186	sized by `FORTRESS_THREADS` (`runtimeSystem/FortressExecutable.java:22-56`).
187	Transactions are static methods on `BaseTask` that generated code calls
188	(`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:180-260`). Both are duplicated: the interpreter
189	has its own independent task and transaction implementations under
190	`interpreter/evaluator/` (`modules-and-phases.md` B.11), so a fix in one is not
191	a fix in the other. Two one-line defects on this side — an eagerly built debug
192	string in `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and a float literal kept as a `String`
193	and re-parsed per use — were repaired on 2026-09-17 and are on record with
194	their before/after numbers (FACTS, execution model).

component XXXOverloadZZ32BesideUserTrait
export Executable

(* A declaration over (ZZ32, ZZ32) beside one over (List, List), List a trait of the program, is a valid overloading, since the one library's ZZ32 is an object, which excludes List, and a call whose arguments are both a SortedList runs the declaration over (SortedList, SortedList) (overloading.tex, section "Incompatibility Rule"). *)

trait List end
trait SortedList extends List end
object PlainL extends List end
object SortedL extends SortedList end

add(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32): ZZ32 = a + b
add(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32, c: ZZ32): ZZ32 = a + b + c
add(a: List, b: List): List = PlainL
add(a: SortedList, b: SortedList): SortedList = SortedL

run(): () = do
  a: List = SortedL
  b: SortedList = SortedL
  r: List = add(a, b)
  k: String = typecase r of
      SortedList => "sorted"
      else => "list"
    end
  assert(k, "sorted", "two SortedList values run add(SortedList, SortedList) (overloading.tex, section \"Overloading Resolution\")")
  assert(add(1, 2), 3, "two ZZ32 run add(ZZ32, ZZ32)")
  assert(add(1, 2, 3), 6, "three ZZ32 run add(ZZ32, ZZ32, ZZ32)")
  println("PASS")
end

end

content.content:
<target name="testFast" depends="compileAll"
          description="Run all unit and system tests expected to pass.">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}"/>
    <!-- The three big suites each dominate a track; everything else shares
         the fourth. Wall clock is the slowest single suite, not the sum. -->
    <parallel threadcount="4">
      <fastTrack id="compiler">
        <include name="**/CompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="library">
        <include name="**/LibraryJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="othercompiler">
        <include name="**/OtherCompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="misc">
        <include name="**/*JUTest.class"/>
        <include name="**/*JUTests.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/CompilerJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/LibraryJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/OtherCompilerJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/OneLibraryJUTest.class"/>

        <!-- Do not run the interpreter tests here. Only run the interpreter
             tests during nightly and CruiseControl testing. -->
        <exclude name="**/TopLevelEnvGenJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/NightlyCompilerJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/SpecDataJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/SystemJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/*$*.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/SyntaxAbstractionJUTestAll.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/ObjectExpressionVisitorJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/tools/AstJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <!-- The compiled path against the one library, under its selection;
           it starts when one of the four above ends. -->
      <fastTrack id="onelibrary" library="one">
        <include name="**/OneLibraryJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
    </parallel>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name="testUntil"
          depends="compileAll"
          description="Run all unit and system tests expected to pass, halting on any errors or failures.">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <junit printsummary="on"
           haltonerror="on"
           haltonfailure="on"
           showoutput="yes"
           fork="true"
           maxmemory="${junitMem}"
           errorProperty="tests.failed"
           failureProperty="tests.failed">
      <classpath refid="compile.classpath"/>
      <jvmarg value="-Djava.io.tmpdir=${PF}/test-tmp" />
      <formatter type="plain" usefile="true"/>
      <batchtest fork="true" todir="${test.results}">
        <fileset dir="${build}">
          <include name="**/*JUTest.class"/>
          <include name="**/*JUTests.class"/>

          <!-- Do not run the interpreter tests here. Only run the interpreter
               tests during nightly and CruiseControl testing. -->
          <exclude name="**/TopLevelEnvGenJUTest.class"/>
          <exclude name="**/NightlyCompilerJUTest.class"/>

          <exclude name="**/*$*.class"/>
          <exclude name="**/SyntaxAbstractionJUTestAll.class"/>
          <exclude name="**/ObjectExpressionVisitorJUTest.class"/>
          <exclude name="**/tools/AstJUTest.class"/>
        </fileset>
      </batchtest>
    </junit>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name="testParser" depends="compileAll"
          description="Run parser tests to debug CruiseControl (Temporary debugging target)">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <junit printsummary="on"
           haltonerror="off"
           haltonfailure="off"
           showoutput="yes"
           fork="true"

(* Each of the seven number types of basic-integers.tex and basic-floats.tex, compiled: its arithmetic, a getter, a typecase arm, a generic box and an overloaded call give their values. *)
component NumberObjectsCompiled
export Executable

object Box[\T extends Object\](v: T)
  get(): T = v
end
unbox[\T extends Object\](b: Box[\T\]): T = b.get()

kind(x: ZZ32): String = "ZZ32"
kind(x: ZZ64): String = "ZZ64"
kind(x: ZZ): String = "ZZ"
kind(x: NN32): String = "NN32"
kind(x: NN64): String = "NN64"
kind(x: RR32): String = "RR32"
kind(x: RR64): String = "RR64"
kind(x: String): String = "String"

arm(x: Any): String = typecase x of
    ZZ => "ZZ"
    ZZ64 => "ZZ64"
    ZZ32 => "ZZ32"
    NN64 => "NN64"
    NN32 => "NN32"
    RR64 => "RR64"
    RR32 => "RR32"
    else => "other"
  end

boxArm(y: Any): String = typecase y of
    Box[\ZZ32\] => "Box of ZZ32"
    Box[\RR64\] => "Box of RR64"
    else => "other box"
  end

run(): () = do
  k: ZZ32 = 3
  m: ZZ32 = k + 4
  assert(m, 7, "ZZ32 +")
  assert(m.asString, "7", "ZZ32 asString")
  assert(k < 5, "ZZ32 <")
  assert(k MAX 9, 9, "ZZ32 MAX")
  assert(k GCD 18, 3, "ZZ32 GCD")
  assert((k CMP 2) = GreaterThan, "ZZ32 CMP")
  assert(arm(k), "ZZ32", "typecase arm at ZZ32")
  assert(kind(k), "ZZ32", "overloaded call at ZZ32")
  assert(unbox(Box[\ZZ32\](5)) + 1, 6, "Box of ZZ32")
  assert(boxArm(Box[\ZZ32\](5)), "Box of ZZ32", "typecase arm at Box of ZZ32")
  var acc: ZZ32 := 0
  for i <- seq(0#10) do acc := acc + i end
  assert(acc, 45, "ZZ32 sum in a loop")

  a: ZZ64 = 3000000000
  assert((a + a) = 6000000000, "ZZ64 +")
  assert((a - 2999999999).asZZ32, 1, "ZZ64 asZZ32")
  assert(arm(a), "ZZ64", "typecase arm at ZZ64")
  assert(kind(a), "ZZ64", "overloaded call at ZZ64")
  assert(unbox(Box[\ZZ64\](a)) = a, "Box of ZZ64")

  z: ZZ = 123456789012345678901234567890
  assert((z + z) = 246913578024691357802469135780, "ZZ +")
  assert(k.asZZ = 3, "ZZ32 asZZ")
  assert(arm(z), "ZZ", "typecase arm at ZZ")
  assert(kind(z), "ZZ", "overloaded call at ZZ")
  assert(unbox(Box[\ZZ\](z)) = z, "Box of ZZ")

  u: NN32 = 7
  assert((u + u) = 14, "NN32 +")
  assert(u.asNN32 = 7, "NN32 asNN32")
  assert(arm(u), "NN32", "typecase arm at NN32")
  assert(kind(u), "NN32", "overloaded call at NN32")
  assert(unbox(Box[\NN32\](u)) = u, "Box of NN32")

  n: NN64 = 5
  assert((n + n) = 10, "NN64 +")
  assert(n.asNN64 = 5, "NN64 asNN64")
  assert(arm(n), "NN64", "typecase arm at NN64")
  assert(kind(n), "NN64", "overloaded call at NN64")
  assert(unbox(Box[\NN64\](n)) = n, "Box of NN64")

  r: RR64 = 1.5
  assert((r r + 0.25) = 2.5, "RR64 juxtaposition and +")
  assert(r < 2.0, "RR64 <")
  assert(NOT r.isNaN, "RR64 isNaN")
  assert((k.asRR64() + r) = 4.5, "ZZ32 asRR64")
  assert(arm(r), "RR64", "typecase arm at RR64")
  assert(kind(r), "RR64", "overloaded call at RR64")
  assert(unbox(Box[\RR64\](r)) = r, "Box of RR64")
  assert(boxArm(Box[\RR64\](r)), "Box of RR64", "typecase arm at Box of RR64")

  f: RR32 = 2.5
  g: RR64 = f + f
  assert(g = 5.0, "RR32 + through RR64")
  assert(f.asString, "2.5", "RR32 asString")
  assert(arm(f), "RR32", "typecase arm at RR32")
  assert(kind(f), "RR32", "overloaded call at RR32")
  h: RR64 = unbox(Box[\RR32\](f))
  assert(h = 2.5, "Box of RR32")
  println("PASS")
end
end
EOF
cd /home/user/fortress-number-payload-objects && export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"

(* A program's object below a built-in number type is refused at load, since the number type is an object. *)
component NumberTypeExtendRefusedWalk
export Executable

object Mine extends ZZ32
    getter asString(): String = "Mine"
    asFloat(self): RR64 = 0.0
end

run(): () = do
    println(Mine.asString)
end

end
load_exception_contains=Attempt to extend object type ZZ32
component OverloadZZ32BesideUserTraitWalk
export Executable

(* A declaration over (ZZ32, ZZ32) beside one over (List, List), List a trait of the program, is a valid overloading, since ZZ32 is an object, which excludes List, and a call whose arguments are both a SortedList runs the declaration over (SortedList, SortedList) (overloading.tex, section "Incompatibility Rule"). *)

content.content:
\subsection{Which objects are value objects}
\seclabel{revival-object-kinds}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] The opening section of \chapref{objects}, its list of
the kinds of objects.
\item[Change] Its sentence on the value objects named booleans, numeric
literals, IEEE floating-point numbers and integers; it now names integers of
every precision and rational numbers too.
Its sentence on the reference objects named arbitrary-precision numbers and
aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets; it now names strings and the
aggregates.
The passage gains one box.
The rule of strict equivalence (\secref{equivalence}) is unchanged: values of
different types are never strictly equivalent, value objects of one type are
when their fields are, a binary word by its bit pattern, and reference objects
only when they are one object.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows two
decisions of the revival.
By the first, of 6~November 2026, the values of the arbitrary-precision integer
and rational types are value objects: \library\ declare the arbitrary-precision
integer as a value object, and the sentence's own list called integers value
objects and arbitrary-precision numbers reference objects, so the text
disagreed with itself and with the library; the library's declaration is the
deliberate word.
By the second, of 6 and 7~November 2026, strictly equivalent means the rule of
\secref{equivalence} on both implementations, with no special case for any type,
and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
object without the \KWD{value} modifier, so two strings are strictly equivalent
only when they are one object, and their text equality is their own \EXP{=}.
The Working Draft of February 2011 named no kind for strings, and the
team's implementations compared two flat strings by their text and two ropes
by identity.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md}, section~2.4, and
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Both implementations answer \EXP{\sequiv} by the rule, and both
read the \KWD{value} modifier.
\Library\ declare the rational type's object as a value object; the numeral
types are traits of which no value exists when a program runs
(\secref{revival-numerals}).
A numeral is converted where it stands on both implementations
(\secref{revival-numerals}), so a floating-point numeral bound to a variable of
type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} is strictly equivalent to a computed \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
value of the same bits, and \EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{x = 3} and
\EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3} on both.
Two string literals of one text are one object (\secref{revival-string-literals}),
so \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''} \sequiv \hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''}} is \VAR{true}, and
a string built as a program runs is not strictly equivalent to an equal literal
unless the operation that builds it answers an existing string.
The departures:
the compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
answers \EXP{\sequiv} on values of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, on strings and on booleans by
\EXP{=} before it
reaches the rule, so there two equal strings built apart are strictly
equivalent and \EXP{0.0} is strictly equivalent to \EXP{-0.0} (row~908 of the
revival's gap ledger);
and \library\ declare \EXP{=} on pairs and triples only, so two tuples of four
or more elements are equal only when they are strictly equivalent, and two such
tuples of equal strings built apart are not equal (row~923 of the revival's
gap ledger).
The answers are gated by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss},
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/ValueObjectCC64Walk.fss} and, for the compiled
helper, by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled.fss}.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/objects.tex},
lines 39--43 and 52--54:
\begin{quote}
Most objects with simple standard types,
such as booleans,
numeric literals,
IEEE floating-point numbers,
and integers are value objects.
\end{quote}
\begin{quote}
Reference objects include
arbitrary-precision numbers
and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
A return to the original sentences would need \library\ to declare the
arbitrary-precision integer and the rational object without the \KWD{value}
modifier, so that two of their values built apart are never strictly
equivalent, and would leave the kind of strings unnamed.
\end{description}

The overview of operators said nothing of either operator's sign or overflow.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

\subsection{The example of coercion resolution}
\seclabel{revival-coercion-example}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{resolving-coercion}.
\item[Change] In the example over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} excludes the two others and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
excludes \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}; the sentence after it names the exclusion and the
rejection from which \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64 \morespecific \mathbb{Z}128} follows, and
says that the same facts make the example's two overloadings valid.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A. The example contradicted
the definition before it: \VAR{T} is no less specific than \VAR{U} only if \VAR{T} is
a subtype of \VAR{U} or excludes, coerces to and rejects \VAR{U}, and without the
clauses \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} neither excludes \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} nor rejects it.
The clauses added are those the definition and the Meet Rule of
\secref{more-specific-rule} need, spelled as \library\ spell the exclusions of
their integer types, each type excluding the wider ones
(\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi}, lines 510--511 and 552--553).
The team's later Types chapter says the same of an \KWD{excludes} clause: an
instantiation of the declared trait ``excludes every type in this set''
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines 344--351,
in the revival's repository).
\item[Effect] The example is a valid program, and both implementations of the revival
run it as printed, the call resolving to \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)}; as the working draft
printed it, both refuse it.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex},
lines 551--552, the first two lines of the example:
\begin{quote}
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64\)
\end{Fortress}
\end{quote}
and lines 562--565:
\begin{quote}
Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the fact that
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

\subsection{The algebra of the rational trait}
\seclabel{revival-rational-algebra}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{basic-rationals}.
\item[Change] The listing of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} extends
\EXP{\TYP{StandardPartialOrder}\llbracket\mathbb{Q}\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{StandardMinMax}\llbracket\mathbb{Q}\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{AdditiveGroup}\llbracket\mathbb{Q}\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{MultiplicativeRing}\llbracket\mathbb{Q}\rrbracket} besides \TYP{Number},
and one sentence after it says that their laws hold for the finite rationals and need
not hold where \EXP{0/0} or an infinity takes part.
\item[Rationale] The number chapters describe the number types that \library\
declare (\secref{revival-numbers}).
at which they could meet are ones that a bound rules out is not settled: the
compiled type checker takes them to exclude where the static argument that the
two parameter types force is a named type that fails the bound, and where a
static parameter that stands at the top of their meet, read as within its
declared bounds, leaves the meet empty, as for row~713's pair, which the
interpreter refuses at load; it reads no bound of a static parameter that
stands inside a static argument (\secref{overloading-static-params}).
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range is
settled (\secref{revival-inference}): it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an
integer numeral does, so the static ranges of \secref{ranges} and the examples
whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds stand as written.
Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
\begin{quote}
The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
library's nested tower today.
They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
behind it.
Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
\seclabel{revival-routec}

The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
instantiations when they form a chain.
The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
type checker and code generator.
Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
types.

"""Generate the probe's shadow sources from the tracked ones by textual patch.

Nothing tracked is modified: the copies are written under <shadow-src>, compiled
into <shadow-classes>, and put FIRST on the run-time classpath, ahead of
ProjectFortress/build.  usage: shadow-patch.py <src-root> <shadow-src>

Three shadows, each one edit:

  DesugarPhase         tolerate a missing type-checker map, so DESUGAR can run
                       with TYPECHECK left out of the phase order (Desugarer
                       passes the map on only to CaseExprDesugarer).
  CodeGenerationPhase  wrap the whole per-component body in try/catch, and print
                       the stack trace of whatever ends it.
  CodeGen              wrap the per-declaration loop of forComponent in
                       try/catch, so one refused declaration does not end the
                       run and the whole hole list comes out of one pass.
"""
import sys, io, os

src, shadow = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]

def patch(rel, edits, out):
    t = io.open(os.path.join(src, rel), encoding="utf-8").read()
    for old, new in edits:
        assert old in t, rel + ": anchor not found: " + old[:60]
        t = t.replace(old, new, 1)
    p = os.path.join(shadow, out)
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(p), exist_ok=True)
    io.open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(t)

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT="$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static"
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

content.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
